instructional_purpose: Trains the learner to convert an agent-naming clause into an agentless one by revocalizing the verb stem and promoting the direct object into a nominative deputy-subject slot, and to recognize why procedural and technical prose prefers the agentless form.
concepts_taught: voice as a vocalization contrast over an unchanged consonantal skeleton
the deputy-subject role نائب الفاعل as the promoted object
agent deletion rather than demotion of the agent to an oblique phrase
perfect-stem passive vocalization
imperfect-stem passive vocalization
passive of two-object verbs and retention of the residual accusative
passive of middle-weak stems
passive of geminate stems
discourse motivations for choosing the agentless form: unknown agent, obvious agent, procedural register, focus on the affected entity, impersonal framing

linguistic_propositions.proposition: In the perfect stem the passive is marked by an u-vowel on the first stem consonant together with an i-vowel before the final consonant.
In the imperfect stem the passive is marked by an u-vowel on the inflectional prefix together with an a-vowel before the final consonant.
The direct object of the active clause surfaces in the passive clause as a nominative deputy subject occupying the position an ordinary subject would occupy.
The Arabic passive removes the agent outright and licenses no agent-naming phrase comparable to an English by-phrase.
With two-object verbs only the first object is promoted and the second stays accusative.
Middle-weak stems realize the passive with a long i-vowel in the perfect and a long a-vowel in the imperfect.
Geminate stems keep their gemination intact under passive vocalization.

recognition_criteria: an u-vowel on the first stem consonant paired with an i-vowel before the final consonant in a perfect verb
an u-vowel on the inflectional prefix paired with an a-vowel before the final consonant in an imperfect verb
a nominative noun immediately following a lexically transitive verb with no agent named anywhere in the clause
a nominative noun followed by a residual accusative, signalling a passivized two-object verb
for middle-weak stems, a long vowel of a quality that the active stem does not show
procedures: locate the agent phrase and delete it
revocalize the verb stem for the tense at hand
recase the former direct object from accusative to nominative
re-check agreement of the verb with the promoted noun
for two-object verbs, promote only the first and leave the second accusative
for middle-weak and geminate stems, apply the class-specific realization instead of the sound-stem template
conditions: only a verb with an available object yields a promoted deputy subject
the text must be vocalized or otherwise disambiguated, since the consonantal skeleton of the two voices is identical for sound stems
the promoted noun must actually carry nominative marking for the transformation to be complete
exceptions: two-object verbs promote only one argument
middle-weak stems do not follow the sound-stem vowel template
geminate stems keep the doubled consonant rather than separating it
contrasts: active vocalization against passive vocalization on the same skeleton
deputy subject against ordinary subject, identical in case but different in derivation
promoted first object against retained second object
Arabic agent deletion against English agent retention in an oblique phrase

common_mistakes.pattern: leaving the promoted noun in the accusative it carried as an object
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the promoted argument occupies a subject position and must be marked nominative
common_mistakes.correction_principle: case follows the syntactic position after promotion, not the position before it

common_mistakes.pattern: using vowel combinations other than the perfect passive template
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the passive is signalled by a fixed vowel pairing, so any other pairing fails to encode voice
common_mistakes.correction_principle: voice is carried by vowel identity and position, not by consonants

common_mistakes.pattern: applying the sound-stem template to a middle-weak stem
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the middle radical of a weak stem is not realized as a consonant carrying a vowel
common_mistakes.correction_principle: select the passive realization by root class before applying any template

common_mistakes.why_wrong: the construction taught here is defined by the absence of a named agent
common_mistakes.correction_principle: if the agent must be named, use an active clause instead of a passive one

assuming voice can be assigned from an unvocalized consonantal string
assuming every nominative after a verb is an ordinary subject

proposed_new_units.summary: A per-stem-class table of passive vocalization for perfect and imperfect, covering sound, middle-weak, final-weak and geminate stems and augmented stems, with an explicit abstention when the surface is unvocalized.

instructional_purpose: Puts a single nominal sentence through every abrogator family in turn so the learner treats each family as a distinct case-assignment operator rather than as vocabulary, and adds the principle that nested abrogators each govern only their own clause.
concepts_taught: the three abrogator families and their differing case signatures
the inverse relation between the كان family and the إنّ family in which component receives accusative
the mental-state family that places both original components in the accusative as first and second object
semantic load per family: temporal and aspectual, modal and epistemic, mental-state
attached pronouns as the carrier of the accusative position with the إنّ family
layering of abrogators and the locality of case assignment
the defective member that has no imperfect form

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Members of the كان family leave the subject nominative and place the predicate in the accusative.
Members of the إنّ family place the subject in the accusative and leave the predicate nominative.
Members of the mental-state family place both the original subject and the original predicate in the accusative as two objects.
The كان family and the إنّ family are exact mirror images of one another.
The membership of each family is a fixed closed list of the size given in the lesson.
With an attached pronoun the accusative of the subject of إنّ is visible on the pronoun itself.
In layered structures each abrogator assigns case only inside its own clause, so assignment is local rather than global.
The negating member of the كان family has only perfect-shaped forms and no imperfect counterpart.

recognition_criteria: identify the head element first, then read its family off a membership list
check which of the two components carries accusative marking to confirm the family
when two accusatives follow a mental-state verb, treat them as a former subject-predicate pair rather than as an object plus a modifier
when an abrogator is embedded under another, close off the inner clause before assigning case
an attached pronoun after an إنّ-family particle occupies the subject position even though it shows no case vowel
procedures: start from the base nominal sentence and label both components
insert the abrogator and re-derive the case of each component from the family signature
restate the resulting semantic value, since the choice of member encodes stance and not only case
for layered structures, bracket each clause and assign case inside the innermost bracket first
conditions: the base structure must be a nominal sentence with an identifiable subject and predicate
case assignment applies only within the clause the abrogator heads
the mental-state family requires a verb that actually takes two objects rather than one
exceptions: the negating member of the كان family lacks an imperfect
attached pronouns are indeclinable and show position rather than case marking
some members of the كان family are licensed only under negation
contrasts: accusative on the predicate against accusative on the subject as the family diagnostic
one accusative against two accusatives
temporal and aspectual meaning against modal and epistemic meaning
wish-marking against hope-marking within the same family
local assignment inside a nested clause against assignment by the outermost head

common_mistakes.pattern: reversing the direction of the case change between the two particle families
common_mistakes.why_wrong: each family has a fixed signature and reversing it produces the signature of the other family
common_mistakes.correction_principle: read the family off the head element before assigning any case

common_mistakes.pattern: carrying one family's rule over to a member of another family
common_mistakes.why_wrong: family membership, not surface similarity, determines the assignment
common_mistakes.correction_principle: resolve membership first, then apply the signature

common_mistakes.pattern: leaving the second component nominative after a mental-state verb
common_mistakes.why_wrong: that family converts both components into objects
common_mistakes.correction_principle: count the arguments the verb takes before assigning case

common_mistakes.pattern: treating the defective negator as an ordinary verb with a full conjugation
common_mistakes.why_wrong: it has no imperfect stem, so any imperfect form of it is invented
common_mistakes.correction_principle: check the paradigm inventory of a frozen or defective item before conjugating it

assuming the listed membership is exhaustive across the grammatical tradition
assuming the case of an attached pronoun can be read off the pronoun form
assuming the outermost head governs everything inside its clause

unpack one layered example clause by clause

nahw_relevance: high — this is a case-assignment system with an explicit locality principle for nesting

proposed_new_units.summary: A licensing table stating, for a clause containing more than one abrogator, which head governs which component, with clause bracketing as the input and an explicit abstention when the bracketing is ambiguous.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-n02 records the per-family case signatures and u-n10 records attachment and scope generally, but neither states which head is responsible for a case when several heads are stacked, which is the claim this lesson actually adds.

instructional_purpose: Teaches number change as a whole-clause operation rather than a change to one word, requiring the learner to propagate a singular, dual or plural choice through the verb, the pronouns, the adjectives and the demonstratives at once.
concepts_taught: the three number categories and their counts
agreement as a chain that must be propagated across every dependent element
verb agreement patterns per number in perfect and imperfect, masculine and feminine
the agreement asymmetry between verb-first and subject-first order
detached and attached pronoun inventories across number
adjective agreement in gender, number, case and definiteness
demonstrative agreement across number for near and far series
dual case marking with two distinct endings
feminine-singular agreement with plurals of non-human referents

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Changing the number of a head noun obliges every element that agrees with it to change as well.
When the verb precedes its subject the verb stays singular regardless of the subject number, and when the subject precedes, full number agreement appears.
Plurals of non-human referents take feminine singular agreement on verbs, adjectives and demonstratives.
The dual carries one ending in the nominative and a different ending in the accusative and genitive, and this alternation applies uniformly to nouns, adjectives and demonstratives.
An adjective must match its head noun simultaneously in gender, number, case and definiteness.
Attached pronouns must be re-selected when the referent changes number, including possessive uses.

recognition_criteria: read the number off the head noun first, then check each dependent for a matching form
use the dual ending to distinguish nominative from the other two cases
check word order before judging a singular verb with a plural subject to be an error
check the human or non-human status of a plural referent before expecting masculine plural agreement
trace attached pronouns back to their referent before deciding they are mismatched
procedures: identify the head noun and its intended new number
convert the head noun, choosing the sound or broken plural stored for that lexeme
convert the demonstrative
convert the adjective for number and case
convert the verb, taking word order into account
convert every attached pronoun whose referent changed
re-check case marking across the whole chain
conditions: the sound or broken plural of the head noun must be known lexically and cannot be derived reliably
agreement targets must be identified before any of them can be converted
the case of the whole phrase determines which dual ending is selected
exceptions: plurals of non-human referents fall out of the ordinary plural agreement pattern
verb-first order suspends number agreement while retaining gender agreement
the first person has no dual form in the pronoun inventory
broken plurals of nouns and of their adjectives are stored, not generated
contrasts: nominative dual ending against the accusative and genitive dual ending
human plural agreement against non-human plural agreement
verb-first agreement against subject-first agreement
sound plural formation against broken plural storage
detached pronoun series against attached pronoun series

common_mistakes.pattern: using a plural verb form ahead of a plural subject
common_mistakes.why_wrong: in verb-first order the verb does not carry number agreement
common_mistakes.correction_principle: decide agreement after fixing word order, not before

common_mistakes.pattern: interchanging the two dual endings
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the endings encode case and are not free variants
common_mistakes.correction_principle: select the dual ending from the case the phrase occupies

common_mistakes.pattern: applying masculine plural agreement to a plural of non-human referents

common_mistakes.correction_principle: check the referent class before selecting an agreement form

common_mistakes.pattern: leaving an attached pronoun singular after its referent has become dual or plural
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the pronoun agrees with the referent and not with the noun it attaches to

misleading_shortcuts: treating the four adjective agreements as literally simultaneous, which the non-human plural rule already breaks

tutor_drill_relevance: high — whole-clause conversion is a strong drill format because a single missed dependent makes the item fail, but the drill must score each dependent separately to be diagnostic

proposed_new_units.summary: A consistency check that, given a head noun with a number, a referent class and a word order, verifies that every dependent verb, adjective, demonstrative and clitic in the clause carries a licensed agreement form, and abstains where the referent of a clitic is undetermined.

instructional_purpose: Teaches the two fixed exclamatory templates, the conditions a verb must satisfy before either template can be built on it, and the workaround construction that routes a disqualified verb through a helper template plus its verbal noun.
concepts_taught: exclamation as a construction distinct from plain predication
the first exclamatory template and the accusative it assigns
the second exclamatory template and the prepositional marking it takes
the six-part condition set licensing direct formation
classes of verbs that fail the conditions: augmented, frozen, colour and defect adjectival, and absolute qualities
the periphrastic route using a helper exclamatory form plus a verbal noun
the admissible shapes of the exclaimed-about element
the literary and archaic distribution of the second template

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A verb must be trilateral, conjugatable, gradable, affirmative, complete and outside the colour and defect adjectival class before an exclamatory template can be built on it directly.
The element exclaimed about in the first template carries accusative marking.
The initial ما of the first template is a particle dedicated to exclamation.
The exclamatory word in the first template is the elative form functioning as a verb.
The noun after the second template is genitive simply because it follows a preposition.
A verb failing the conditions can still be exclaimed about by combining a licensed helper form with the verbal noun of the disqualified verb.
The second template is archaic and literary rather than conversational.

recognition_criteria: a clause-initial ما followed immediately by a fixed elative-shaped word and an accusative noun
an imperative-shaped word of the elative pattern followed by a prepositional phrase with no addressee in context
a helper exclamatory form followed by a verbal noun, signalling the indirect route
the exclaimed-about element appearing as a definite noun, a possessed noun, a demonstrative phrase, an indefinite noun or a verbal noun
procedures: identify the root and check it against the six conditions
if licensed, build the elative shape and place the exclaimed element in the accusative for the first template
or build the imperative-shaped form and attach the element with the fixed preposition for the second template
if not licensed, select a helper form appropriate to the semantic dimension and follow it with the verbal noun of the intended verb

the verb must inflect rather than be frozen
the quality must admit degrees
the verb must be affirmative and complete
the derived adjective must not belong to the colour and defect pattern
exceptions: augmented stems are routed through the periphrastic construction
frozen verbs cannot enter either template
colour and defect verbs are routed through the periphrastic construction
qualities that admit no degrees are treated as not exclaimable in the standard way
contrasts: plain predication against exclamation of the same quality
accusative marking in the first template against prepositional marking in the second
direct formation against periphrastic formation
the everyday first template against the archaic second template
imperative form against imperative function in the second template

instructional_purpose: Teaches the conversion of quoted speech into reported speech, treating the operation as a coordinated re-anchoring of person, place and time deixis under a reporting frame rather than as the insertion of a single particle.
concepts_taught: quoted against reported speech as two framings of the same content
person shift across detached and attached pronouns
spatial and temporal deixis shift under reporting
tense handling that does not require a mechanical backshift
an inventory of reporting verbs and the complementizer each selects
the division of labour between the two subordinating particles
reporting of polar questions, content questions and commands

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Converting quoted speech to reported speech requires re-anchoring first and second person forms to the reporter perspective, including possessive clitics.
Near demonstratives and proximal place and time adverbs shift to their distal counterparts under reporting.
Arabic does not require the tense backshift that English reporting requires, so an imperfect may be retained unchanged.
The emphatic particle introduces the reported clause after the verb of saying, while the subordinating particle is selected after other reporting verbs.
Attaching the subordinating particle to the verb of saying by way of a preposition is non-standard.
Reported polar questions are introduced by a conditional-shaped complementizer or by the polar interrogative particle.
Reported commands are expressed with the subjunctive complementizer plus a subjunctive verb.
Both subordinating particles place their subject in the accusative and leave their predicate nominative.

recognition_criteria: a reporting verb followed by a complementizer marks the boundary of reported content
a third-person pronoun immediately after the complementizer is a candidate for the original speaker rather than for a new referent
a distal demonstrative inside reported content may correspond to a proximal one in the original utterance
the choice of complementizer signals which reporting verb heads the frame
an interrogative word retained inside a reported clause signals a reported content question rather than a direct one
procedures: identify the original speaker, the addressee and the reporter
shift every first and second person form to the perspective of the reporter
shift proximal deictics where the reporting context is displaced
select a reporting verb and its licensed complementizer

linguistic_propositions.proposition: These praise and blame items are verbs that are frozen in a single form and never inflect for tense, person, number or gender.
A complete praise or blame clause has three slots: the frozen item, a subject naming a category, and a following element naming the specific referent.
The subject must be definite by the article, a generic indefinite, or a relative clause headed by one of the two general relatives.
The specified element is nominative regardless of which of the two classical analyses is adopted.
The compound praise item has its subject incorporated into it and therefore takes no separate subject.
The specified element may be omitted when the referent is fully recoverable from context.
The two blame items share one structure and differ only in emphasis and frequency.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A single root yields a finite verb, a verbal noun and an active participle that share lexical content but differ in what they foreground.
The verb foregrounds a time-anchored action, the verbal noun foregrounds the event as an abstract entity, and the participle foregrounds the identity of the agent.
When a clause is nominalized around a verbal noun, the former subject becomes the genitive second term of a possessive construction.
A verbal noun may govern a direct object in the accusative exactly as its verb does, and this construction is formal and literary.
Attaching the object with a preposition avoids the accusative-after-possessive construction.
The active participle of a final-weak root drops its final weak letter before indefinite nominative and genitive marking and shows it in the accusative and in definite forms.
The root cited as the survival example is classified as a hollow verb.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The emphatic particle raises the formality of the clause it heads in addition to adding assertive force.
The emphatic particle places its subject in the accusative.
The emphatic form heads independent assertions while the subordinating form heads embedded clauses.
Vernacular varieties omit or simplify the abrogator particles, and this omission is a reliable marker of informal register.
One propositional content can be expressed at every level of the register scale, and speakers select a level from context, audience and emotional state.
Each sister of the emphatic particle carries its own register effect, from formal contrast to literary comparison to elevated wish.
The formal death announcement in the register table is a passive verb form.
